claim: K-Ras4a is subject to lysine fatty acylation.
source: Here we report that one of the K-Ras splice variants, K-Ras4a, is subject to lysine fatty acylation, a previously under-studied protein post-translational modification.
evidence: Supported by experimental data including Alk14 metabolic labeling, mass spectrometry identification of fatty acylation on K182, and NH2OH-resistant fatty acylation assays shown in Figures 1 and 3.

claim: SIRT2 catalyzes the removal of fatty acylation from K-Ras4a.
source: Sirtuin 2 (SIRT2), one of the mammalian nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD)-dependent lysine deacylases, catalyzes the removal of fatty acylation from K-Ras4a.
evidence: Demonstrated by in vitro defatty-acylation assays, SIRT2 knockdown experiments showing increased K-Ras4a lysine fatty acylation, and 32P-NAD assays shown in Figure 2.

claim: SIRT2-mediated lysine defatty-acylation promotes endomembrane localization of K-Ras4a.
source: We further demonstrate that SIRT2-mediated lysine defatty-acylation promotes endomembrane localization of K-Ras4a, enhances its interaction with A-Raf, and thus promotes cellular transformation.
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy data showing that SIRT2 KD decreased intracellular punctate localization of K-Ras4a-WT but not the 3KR mutant, and colocalization analyses with endomembrane markers shown in Figure 4.

claim: SIRT2-mediated lysine defatty-acylation enhances K-Ras4a interaction with A-Raf.
source: We further demonstrate that SIRT2-mediated lysine defatty-acylation promotes endomembrane localization of K-Ras4a, enhances its interaction with A-Raf, and thus promotes cellular transformation.
evidence: Demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments showing that SIRT2 KD decreased A-Raf binding to K-Ras4a-G12V but not to K-Ras4a-G12V-3KR, and live cell imaging showing enhanced endomembrane colocalization of A-Raf with K-Ras4a-3KR shown in Figure 6.

claim: SIRT2-mediated lysine defatty-acylation promotes cellular transformation by K-Ras4a.
source: We further demonstrate that SIRT2-mediated lysine defatty-acylation promotes endomembrane localization of K-Ras4a, enhances its interaction with A-Raf, and thus promotes cellular transformation.
evidence: Supported by soft agar colony formation assays showing that SIRT2 KD more potently inhibited K-Ras4a-G12V-mediated colony formation than K-Ras4a-G12V-3KR-mediated colony formation shown in Figure 5.

claim: Lysine fatty acylation is a previously unknown regulatory mechanism for the Ras family of GTPases.
source: Our study identifies lysine fatty acylation as a previously unknown regulatory mechanism for the Ras family of GTPases that is distinct from cysteine fatty acylation.
evidence: Based on the novel finding that K-Ras4a is regulated by lysine fatty acylation, which is distinct from the well-characterized cysteine palmitoylation of Ras proteins.

claim: Ras proteins play vital roles in numerous biological processes.
source: Ras proteins play vital roles in numerous biological processes and Ras mutations are found in many human tumors.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about Ras proteins.

claim: Ras mutations are found in many human tumors.
source: Ras proteins play vital roles in numerous biological processes and Ras mutations are found in many human tumors.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about Ras proteins and cancer.

claim: Protein fatty acylation facilitates direct association of proteins with particular membranes in cells.
source: Protein fatty acylation facilitates direct association of proteins with particular membranes in cells and plays a vital role in protein trafficking, cell signaling, protein-protein interactions, and protein activity (Lanyon-Hogg et al., 2017; Peng et al., 2016; Tate et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Protein fatty acylation plays a vital role in protein trafficking, cell signaling, protein-protein interactions, and protein activity.
source: Protein fatty acylation facilitates direct association of proteins with particular membranes in cells and plays a vital role in protein trafficking, cell signaling, protein-protein interactions, and protein activity (Lanyon-Hogg et al., 2017; Peng et al., 2016; Tate et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Dysregulation of protein fatty acylation is implicated in human cancer and neurodegenerative diseases.
source: Dysregulation of protein fatty acylation is implicated in human cancer and neurodegenerative diseases (Lanyon-Hogg et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The biological function of protein lysine fatty acylation is not clear.
source: Although first reported over two decades ago, the biological function of protein lysine fatty acylation is not clear and to date, only a few proteins, such as tumor necrosis factor α (TNF-α) and interleukin 1-α, are known to be regulated by lysine fatty acylation (Bursten et al., 1988; Hedo et al., 1987; Pillai and Baltimore, 1987; Stevenson et al., 1993; Stevenson et al., 1992).
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field, supported by citations.

claim: TNF-α and interleukin 1-α are known to be regulated by lysine fatty acylation.
source: Although first reported over two decades ago, the biological function of protein lysine fatty acylation is not clear and to date, only a few proteins, such as tumor necrosis factor α (TNF-α) and interleukin 1-α, are known to be regulated by lysine fatty acylation (Bursten et al., 1988; Hedo et al., 1987; Pillai and Baltimore, 1987; Stevenson et al., 1993; Stevenson et al., 1992).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Several sirtuins can act as lysine defatty-acylases.
source: The enzymes that catalyze the addition or removal of lysine fatty acylation were not known until recently when we and others found that several sirtuins, the nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD)-dependent protein lysine deacylase, could act as lysine defatty-acylase.
evidence: This is a statement about recent discoveries in the field.

claim: TNF-α secretion is regulated by SIRT6-catalyzed removal of lysine fatty acylation.
source: We have previously reported that TNF-α (Jiang et al., 2013; Jiang et al., 2016) and exosome (Zhang et al., 2016) secretion are regulated by sirtuin 6 (SIRT6)-catalyzed removal of lysine fatty acylation, demonstrating that lysine fatty acylation is reversible and physiologically important.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: Exosome secretion is regulated by SIRT6-catalyzed removal of lysine fatty acylation.
source: We have previously reported that TNF-α (Jiang et al., 2013; Jiang et al., 2016) and exosome (Zhang et al., 2016) secretion are regulated by sirtuin 6 (SIRT6)-catalyzed removal of lysine fatty acylation, demonstrating that lysine fatty acylation is reversible and physiologically important.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: Lysine fatty acylation is reversible and physiologically important.
source: We have previously reported that TNF-α (Jiang et al., 2013; Jiang et al., 2016) and exosome (Zhang et al., 2016) secretion are regulated by sirtuin 6 (SIRT6)-catalyzed removal of lysine fatty acylation, demonstrating that lysine fatty acylation is reversible and physiologically important.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the previous findings cited.

claim: SIRT1-3 and SIRT7 can efficiently remove fatty acyl groups from lysine residues in vitro.
source: Other sirtuin family proteins, SIRT1-3 (Bao et al., 2014; Feldman et al., 2013; He et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2015; Teng et al., 2015) and SIRT7 (Tong et al., 2017) have also been found to efficiently remove fatty acyl groups from lysine residues in vitro, suggesting that lysine fatty acylation may be more prevalent.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Lysine fatty acylation may be more prevalent than previously thought.
source: Other sirtuin family proteins, SIRT1-3 (Bao et al., 2014; Feldman et al., 2013; He et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2015; Teng et al., 2015) and SIRT7 (Tong et al., 2017) have also been found to efficiently remove fatty acyl groups from lysine residues in vitro, suggesting that lysine fatty acylation may be more prevalent.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the finding that multiple sirtuins can remove lysine fatty acylation.

claim: Ras proteins are small GTPases that play important roles in numerous tumor-driving processes.
source: Ras proteins are small GTPases that play important roles in numerous tumor-driving processes, including proliferation, differentiation, survival, cell cycle entry and cytoskeletal dynamics (Malumbres and Barbacid, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Ras proteins act as binary switches: they are active when GTP is bound and inactive in the GDP-bound state.
source: They act as binary switches: they are active when GTP is bound, turning on specific signaling pathways by recruiting effector proteins, and inactive in the GDP-bound state (Hancock, 2003; Malumbres and Barbacid, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Guanine nucleotide exchange factors (GEFs) activate Ras by promoting GDP-GTP exchange.
source: Guanine nucleotide exchange factors (GEFs) activate Ras by promoting GDP-GTP exchange, whereas GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs) inactivate Ras by promoting intrinsic GTP hydrolysis (Malumbres and Barbacid, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs) inactivate Ras by promoting intrinsic GTP hydrolysis.
source: Guanine nucleotide exchange factors (GEFs) activate Ras by promoting GDP-GTP exchange, whereas GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs) inactivate Ras by promoting intrinsic GTP hydrolysis (Malumbres and Barbacid, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: In mammals, HRAS, NRAS, and KRAS proto-oncogenes encode four proteins: H-Ras, N-Ras, K-Ras4a, and K-Ras4b.
source: In mammals, HRAS, NRAS, and KRAS proto-oncogenes encode four proteins: H-Ras, N-Ras, K-Ras4a, and K-Ras4b.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Ras proteins.

claim: K-Ras4a and K-Ras4b are the two splice variants encoded by the KRAS gene.
source: K-Ras4a and K-Ras4b are the two splice variants encoded by the KRAS gene.
evidence: This is established knowledge about K-Ras isoforms.

claim: K-Ras4b was assumed to be the more abundant and thus the more important K-Ras isoform mutated in human cancers.
source: K-Ras4b has attracted most of the attention because it was assumed to be the more abundant and thus the more important K-Ras isoform mutated in human cancers.
evidence: This is a statement about historical assumptions in the field.

claim: K-Ras4a is widely expressed in many cancer cell lines.
source: However, recent studies have revealed that K-Ras4a is widely expressed in many cancer cell lines and its level is similar to that of K-Ras4b in human colorectal tumors (Tsai et al., 2015; Zhao et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to recent literature.

claim: K-Ras4a level is similar to that of K-Ras4b in human colorectal tumors.
source: However, recent studies have revealed that K-Ras4a is widely expressed in many cancer cell lines and its level is similar to that of K-Ras4b in human colorectal tumors (Tsai et al., 2015; Zhao et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to recent literature.

claim: Oncogenic K-Ras4a is required for lung carcinogenesis in mice.
source: A requirement for oncogenic K-Ras4a in lung carcinogenesis has also been demonstrated in mice (To et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: There is increasing interest in evaluating K-Ras4a as a therapeutic target.
source: Thus, there is increasing interest in evaluating K-Ras4a as a therapeutic target and in investigating the regulation of K-Ras4a.
evidence: This is an inference based on the recent findings about K-Ras4a expression and function.

claim: Ras proteins exert their functions at cellular membranes.
source: Ras proteins exert their functions at cellular membranes, where they interact with distinct effectors and activate downstream signaling (Hancock, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: All four Ras proteins are modified by cysteine farnesylation on their CaaX motif.
source: All four Ras proteins are modified by cysteine farnesylation on their CaaX motif.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Ras protein modifications.

claim: H-Ras and N-Ras contain cysteine palmitoylation as the second membrane targeting signal.
source: H-Ras and N-Ras contain cysteine palmitoylation as the second membrane targeting signal, whereas K-Ras4b uses a polybasic region (PBR) (Figure 1a).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 1a and established knowledge.

claim: K-Ras4b uses a polybasic region (PBR) as the second membrane targeting signal.
source: H-Ras and N-Ras contain cysteine palmitoylation as the second membrane targeting signal, whereas K-Ras4b uses a polybasic region (PBR) (Figure 1a).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 1a and established knowledge.

claim: K-Ras4a possesses a hybrid membrane targeting motif: multiple lysine residues at the C-terminus as well as cysteine palmitoylation.
source: K-Ras4a possesses a hybrid membrane targeting motif: multiple lysine residues at the C-terminus (similar to K-Ras4b) as well as cysteine palmitoylation (Figure 1a) (Tsai et al., 2015; Zhao et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 1a and citations to previous literature.

claim: H-Ras, N-Ras, and K-Ras4a retained 20%, 13% and 47% NH2OH-resistant fatty acylation over total fatty acylation, respectively.
source: Quantification of the fluorescent signal revealed that NH2OH treatment removed over 95% of the fatty acylation from RalA or STX6. However, H-Ras, N-Ras, and K-Ras4a retained 20%, 13% and 47% NH2OH-resistant fatty acylation over total fatty acylation, respectively, whereas K-Ras4b did not show Alk14 labeling either before or after NH2OH treatment (Figure 1c).
evidence: Supported by quantification of in-gel fluorescence data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: K-Ras4b did not show Alk14 labeling either before or after NH2OH treatment.
source: Quantification of the fluorescent signal revealed that NH2OH treatment removed over 95% of the fatty acylation from RalA or STX6. However, H-Ras, N-Ras, and K-Ras4a retained 20%, 13% and 47% NH2OH-resistant fatty acylation over total fatty acylation, respectively, whereas K-Ras4b did not show Alk14 labeling either before or after NH2OH treatment (Figure 1c).
evidence: Supported by in-gel fluorescence data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: H-Ras, N-Ras, and K-Ras4a might possess non-cysteine fatty acylation.
source: These data suggest that H-Ras, N-Ras, and K-Ras4a might possess non-cysteine fatty acylation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the NH2OH-resistant fatty acylation observed in Figure 1c.

claim: H-Ras K170 is modified by fatty acylation.
source: This allowed us to identify H-Ras K170 (Figure 1g) and K-Ras4a K182 (Figure 1h) as being modified, confirming lysine fatty acylation of H-Ras and K-Ras4a.
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1g.

claim: K-Ras4a K182 is modified by fatty acylation.
source: This allowed us to identify H-Ras K170 (Figure 1g) and K-Ras4a K182 (Figure 1h) as being modified, confirming lysine fatty acylation of H-Ras and K-Ras4a.
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1h.

claim: PfSir2A can remove most of the NH2OH-resistant fatty acylation from H-Ras and K-Ras4a in the presence of NAD.
source: Incubation of H-Ras or K-Ras4a with Plasmodium falciparum Sir2A (PfSir2A), a sirtuin family member with robust lysine defatty-acylase activity (Zhu et al., 2012), resulted in the removal of most of the NH2OH-resistant fatty acylation from H-Ras and K-Ras4a in the presence of NAD (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Supported by in vitro defatty-acylation assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a.

claim: The NH2OH-resistant fatty acylation of H-Ras and K-Ras4a is mainly from lysine residues.
source: This result further confirmed that the NH2OH-resistant fatty acylation is mainly from lysine residues and indicated that lysine fatty acylation of H-Ras and K-Ras4a is reversible.
evidence: This is an inference based on the PfSir2A defatty-acylation results.

claim: Lysine fatty acylation of H-Ras and K-Ras4a is reversible.
source: This result further confirmed that the NH2OH-resistant fatty acylation is mainly from lysine residues and indicated that lysine fatty acylation of H-Ras and K-Ras4a is reversible.
evidence: This is an inference based on the PfSir2A defatty-acylation results showing enzymatic removal of lysine fatty acylation.

claim: SIRT2 slightly decreased the lysine fatty acylation signal of H-Ras.
source: Furthermore, SIRT2, but not SIRT1, 3, or 6, slightly decreased the lysine fatty acylation signal of H-Ras (Figure 2a); SIRT1 and SIRT2, but not SIRT3 and SIRT6, removed lysine fatty acylation from K-Ras4a.
evidence: Supported by in vitro defatty-acylation assay data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: SIRT1 and SIRT2 removed lysine fatty acylation from K-Ras4a.
source: Furthermore, SIRT2, but not SIRT1, 3, or 6, slightly decreased the lysine fatty acylation signal of H-Ras (Figure 2a); SIRT1 and SIRT2, but not SIRT3 and SIRT6, removed lysine fatty acylation from K-Ras4a.
evidence: Supported by in vitro defatty-acylation assay data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: SIRT2 showed better activity than SIRT1 on K-Ras4a lysine fatty acylation.
source: Notably, SIRT2 showed better activity than SIRT1 on K-Ras4a lysine fatty acylation (Figure 2b).
evidence: Supported by comparison of in vitro defatty-acylation assay data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: SIRT1 and SIRT2 do not possess cysteine defatty-acylase activity.
source: In contrast, SIRT1 and SIRT2 showed little effect on the fatty acylation of K-Ras4a-3KR (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b), which exhibited significantly lower lysine fatty acylation than K-Ras4a-WT (Figure 1f), suggesting that SIRT1 and SIRT2 do not possess cysteine defatty-acylase activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of effect of SIRT1 and SIRT2 on K-Ras4a-3KR fatty acylation shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b.

claim: SIRT2 was unable to remove the cysteine myristoyl group from a K-Ras4a-C180myr peptide.
source: An HPLC-based in vitro activity assay also revealed that SIRT2 was unable to remove the cysteine myristoyl group from a K-Ras4a-C180myr peptide (Figure 2—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: Supported by HPLC-based in vitro activity assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1c.

claim: Knockdown of SIRT2 in HEK293T cells did not affect lysine fatty acylation of H-Ras.
source: Furthermore, knockdown (KD) of SIRT2 in HEK293T cells did not affect lysine fatty acylation of H-Ras (Figure 2c and f), whereas KD of SIRT2 but not SIRT1 significantly increased lysine fatty acylation of K-Ras4a compared with control (Ctrl) KD (Figure 2d,e and f).
evidence: Supported by Alk14 labeling and in-gel fluorescence data shown in Figure 2c and f.

claim: Knockdown of SIRT2 but not SIRT1 significantly increased lysine fatty acylation of K-Ras4a compared with control KD.
source: Furthermore, knockdown (KD) of SIRT2 in HEK293T cells did not affect lysine fatty acylation of H-Ras (Figure 2c and f), whereas KD of SIRT2 but not SIRT1 significantly increased lysine fatty acylation of K-Ras4a compared with control (Ctrl) KD (Figure 2d,e and f).
evidence: Supported by Alk14 labeling and in-gel fluorescence data shown in Figure 2d, e and f.

claim: K-Ras4a is a lysine defatty-acylation substrate for SIRT2 in cells.
source: Taken together, these results illustrate that K-Ras4a is a lysine defatty-acylation substrate for SIRT2 in cells, but H-Ras and N-Ras are not.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined results from in vitro and cellular assays shown in Figure 2.

claim: H-Ras and N-Ras are not lysine defatty-acylation substrates for SIRT2 in cells.
source: Taken together, these results illustrate that K-Ras4a is a lysine defatty-acylation substrate for SIRT2 in cells, but H-Ras and N-Ras are not.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined results from in vitro and cellular assays shown in Figure 2.

claim: Co-expression of SIRT2 with K-Ras4a in HEK293T cells substantially decreased K-Ras4a lysine fatty acylation.
source: Co-expression of SIRT2 with K-Ras4a in HEK293T cells substantially decreased K-Ras4a lysine fatty acylation, whereas co-expression of SIRT2-HY had much less effect (Figure 2g), suggesting that K-Ras4a defatty-acylation requires SIRT2 catalytic activity.
evidence: Supported by Alk14 labeling and in-gel fluorescence data shown in Figure 2g.

claim: Co-expression of SIRT2-HY with K-Ras4a had much less effect on K-Ras4a lysine fatty acylation than SIRT2-WT.
source: Co-expression of SIRT2 with K-Ras4a in HEK293T cells substantially decreased K-Ras4a lysine fatty acylation, whereas co-expression of SIRT2-HY had much less effect (Figure 2g), suggesting that K-Ras4a defatty-acylation requires SIRT2 catalytic activity.
evidence: Supported by Alk14 labeling and in-gel fluorescence data shown in Figure 2g.

claim: K-Ras4a defatty-acylation requires SIRT2 catalytic activity.
source: Co-expression of SIRT2 with K-Ras4a in HEK293T cells substantially decreased K-Ras4a lysine fatty acylation, whereas co-expression of SIRT2-HY had much less effect (Figure 2g), suggesting that K-Ras4a defatty-acylation requires SIRT2 catalytic activity.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of SIRT2-WT and SIRT2-HY effects shown in Figure 2g.

claim: Acetylation was not detected on K-Ras4a in either Ctrl KD or SIRT2 KD cells without or with histone deacetylases (HDAC) inhibitor Trichostatin A (TSA).
source: Acetylation was not detected on K-Ras4a in either Ctrl KD or SIRT2 KD cells without or with histone deacetylases (HDAC) inhibitor Trichostatin A (TSA) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1f).
evidence: Supported by western blot data using anti-acetyllysine antibody shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1f.

claim: SIRT2 likely does not regulate K-Ras4a via deacetylation.
source: We also searched our K-Ras4a MS data and did not find any peptides with lysine acetylation, indicating that SIRT2 likely does not regulate K-Ras4a via deacetylation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of acetylation detection by western blot and mass spectrometry.

claim: K-Ras4a contains lysine fatty acylation that can be removed by SIRT2 in the absence of Alk14 supplementation.
source: These results demonstrate that K-Ras4a contains lysine fatty acylation that can be removed by SIRT2 in the absence of Alk14 supplementation.
evidence: Supported by the 32P-NAD assay results shown in Figure 2h.

claim: Palmitoylation is the major native lysine acylation of K-Ras4a.
source: A peptide carrying palmitoylation, but not myristoylation, on K182 of FLAG-tagged K-Ras4a was detected by MS (Figure 2—figure supplement 1g), demonstrating that palmitoylation is the major native lysine acylation of K-Ras4a.
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1g.

claim: Endogenous K-Ras4a is regulated by SIRT2-catalyzed lysine defatty-acylation.
source: This result, together with the detection of K-Ras4a lysine fatty acylation by Alk14 biotinylation, further supports that endogenous K-Ras4a is lysine fatty acylated and is regulated by SIRT2-mediated lysine defatty-acylation.
evidence: Supported by biotin pull-down assay data shown in Figure 2i and total Ras fatty acylation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2a and b.

claim: SIRT2 was present in both soluble and membrane fractions.
source: Indeed, by subcellular fractionation, we found that SIRT2 was present in both soluble and membrane fractions (Figure 2—figure supplement 1h).
evidence: Supported by subcellular fractionation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1h.

claim: K-Ras4a associated with endogenous SIRT2.
source: Co-immunoprecipitation (co-IP) revealed K-Ras4a associated with endogenous SIRT2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1i).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1i.

claim: K182, 184 and 185 of K-Ras4a are likely to be modified redundantly by fatty acylation.
source: These results suggested that K182, 184 and 185 were likely to be modified redundantly.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mutagenesis results showing that individual K to R mutations did not significantly decrease lysine fatty acylation as much as the 3KR mutant.

claim: The K182A mutation did not affect overall level of K-Ras4a lysine fatty acylation.
source: As expected, the K182A mutation did not affect overall level of K-Ras4a lysine fatty acylation (Figure 3b).
evidence: Supported by Alk14 labeling and in-gel fluorescence data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: A peptide fatty acylated on K184 was detected by MS for K-Ras4a-K182A.
source: A peptide (amino acids 177–185) fatty acylated on K184 was detected by MS (Figure 3b), which agrees with our hypothesis.
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: K182/184/185 of K-Ras4a are fatty acylated redundantly.
source: Overall, these data indicate that K182/184/185 are fatty acylated redundantly and that the 3KR mutation is needed to abolish lysine fatty acylation on the C-terminus of K-Ras4a.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined mutagenesis and mass spectrometry results shown in Figure 3.

claim: The 3KR mutation is needed to abolish lysine fatty acylation on the C-terminus of K-Ras4a.
source: Overall, these data indicate that K182/184/185 are fatty acylated redundantly and that the 3KR mutation is needed to abolish lysine fatty acylation on the C-terminus of K-Ras4a.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined mutagenesis and mass spectrometry results shown in Figure 3.

claim: Mutation of the prenylcysteine (C186S) completely abolished the fatty acylation of K-Ras4a.
source: Mutation of the prenylcysteine (C186S) completely abolished the fatty acylation of K-Ras4a (Figure 3c), which is consistent with the model that prenylation of the cysteine on the CaaX motif of Ras proteins is required for the subsequent fatty acylation (Wright and Philips, 2006).
evidence: Supported by Alk14 labeling and in-gel fluorescence data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: Mutation of the palmitoylated cysteine (C180S) led to a substantial, but not a complete, loss of K-Ras4a lysine fatty acylation.
source: On the other hand, mutation of the palmitoylated cysteine (C180S) led to a substantial, but not a complete, loss of K-Ras4a lysine fatty acylation (Figure 3c).
evidence: Supported by Alk14 labeling and in-gel fluorescence data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: The fatty acylation on the C180S mutant was NH2OH-resistant and was abolished by combining the C180S and 3KR mutations.
source: The fatty acylation on the C180S mutant was NH2OH-resistant and was abolished by combining the C180S and 3KR mutations (Figure 3d), implying that the C180S mutant was fatty acylated on K182/184/185.
evidence: Supported by Alk14 labeling and in-gel fluorescence data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Cysteine palmitoylation might play an important but nonessential role in the occurrence of lysine fatty acylation.
source: These data suggest that cysteine palmitoylation might play an important but nonessential role in the occurrence of lysine fatty acylation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that C180S mutation substantially but not completely abolished lysine fatty acylation.

claim: SIRT2 removed lysine fatty acylation from K-Ras4a-WT, the 4KR mutant, and the C180S mutant, but not the 3KR mutant in vitro.
source: SIRT2 removed lysine fatty acylation from K-Ras4a-WT, the 4KR mutant, and the C180S mutant, but not the 3KR mutant in vitro (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a and b).
evidence: Supported by in vitro defatty-acylation assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a and b.

claim: SIRT2 KD in HEK293T cells increased lysine fatty acylation of K-Ras4a-WT and the C180S mutant, but not the 3KR and C180S-3KR mutants.
source: SIRT2 KD in HEK293T cells increased lysine fatty acylation of K-Ras4a-WT and the C180S mutant, but not the 3KR and C180S-3KR mutants (Figure 3e).
evidence: Supported by Alk14 labeling and in-gel fluorescence data shown in Figure 3e.

claim: Fatty acylation on K182/184/185 is regulated by SIRT2.
source: These data indicate that fatty acylation on K182/184/185 is regulated by SIRT2.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined in vitro and cellular assay results shown in Figure 3.

claim: SIRT2 KD decreased the intracellular punctate-localized K-Ras4a-WT compared to Ctrl KD.
source: SIRT2 KD decreased the intracellular punctate-localized K-Ras4a-WT compared to Ctrl KD, whereas it had no effect on the punctate localization of the 3KR mutant (Figure 4a and b) that did not contain SIRT2-regulated lysine fatty acylation.
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4a and b.

claim: SIRT2 KD had no effect on the punctate localization of the K-Ras4a-3KR mutant.
source: SIRT2 KD decreased the intracellular punctate-localized K-Ras4a-WT compared to Ctrl KD, whereas it had no effect on the punctate localization of the 3KR mutant (Figure 4a and b) that did not contain SIRT2-regulated lysine fatty acylation.
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4a and b.

claim: SIRT2-catalyzed lysine defatty-acylation promotes the intracellular punctate localization of K-Ras4a.
source: This result suggests that SIRT2-catalyzed lysine defatty-acylation promotes the intracellular punctate localization of K-Ras4a and that the K-Ras4a-3KR mutant has increased intracellular punctate localization mainly due to the lack of lysine fatty acylation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the confocal microscopy results shown in Figure 4a and b.

claim: The K-Ras4a-3KR mutant has increased intracellular punctate localization mainly due to the lack of lysine fatty acylation.
source: This result suggests that SIRT2-catalyzed lysine defatty-acylation promotes the intracellular punctate localization of K-Ras4a and that the K-Ras4a-3KR mutant has increased intracellular punctate localization mainly due to the lack of lysine fatty acylation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the confocal microscopy results shown in Figure 4a and b.

claim: SIRT2 KD did not affect the intracellular punctate localization of H-Ras.
source: On the other hand, SIRT2 KD did not affect the intracellular punctate localization of H-Ras (Figure 4a and b), which is consistent with our observation that H-Ras was not regulated by SIRT2 through lysine defatty-acylation.
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4a and b.

claim: Lysine fatty acylation inhibits the intracellular punctate localization of K-Ras4a.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that lysine fatty acylation inhibits the intracellular punctate localization of K-Ras4a and SIRT2 promotes this localization by defatty-acylation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined confocal microscopy results shown in Figure 4.

claim: SIRT2 promotes intracellular punctate localization of K-Ras4a by defatty-acylation.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that lysine fatty acylation inhibits the intracellular punctate localization of K-Ras4a and SIRT2 promotes this localization by defatty-acylation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined confocal microscopy results shown in Figure 4.

claim: The K-Ras4a-3KR mutant exhibited more pronounced cytoplasmic colocalization with trans-Golgi network (TGN) marker STX6, early endosome marker EEA1, recycling endosome marker Rab11, and lysosome marker LAMP1 compared with K-Ras4a-WT.
source: Compared with K-Ras4a-WT, the 3KR mutant exhibited more pronounced cytoplasmic colocalization with trans-Golgi network (TGN) marker STX6, early endosome marker EEA1, recycling endosome marker Rab11, and lysosome marker LAMP1 (Figure 4c and d), but not with the ER marker Sec61, trans-Golgi marker GalT and late endosome marker Rab7 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1h and i).
evidence: Supported by colocalization analyses shown in Figure 4c and d.

claim: Removal of lysine fatty acylation from K-Ras4a promotes its localization to endomembranes in endocytic pathways.
source: These results suggest that removal of lysine fatty acylation from K-Ras4a promotes its localization to endomembranes in endocytic pathways, by which it may be routed from early endosome to the lysosome for degradation and to the TGN or recycling endosomes to return to the plasma membrane (Grant and Donaldson, 2009).
evidence: This is an inference based on the colocalization analyses shown in Figure 4c and d, combined with knowledge of endocytic pathways.

claim: Expression of K-Ras4a-G12V-3KR resulted in significantly more colony formation on soft agar than did expression of K-Ras4a-G12V in Ctrl KD cells.
source: In Ctrl KD cells, expression of K-Ras4a-G12V-3KR resulted in significantly more colony formation on soft agar than did expression of K-Ras4a-G12V.
evidence: Supported by soft agar colony formation assay data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Sirt2 KD caused a greater decrease in colony formation induced by K-Ras4a-G12V (75% decrease) than by K-Ras4a-G12V-3KR (45% decrease).
source: Furthermore, Sirt2 KD caused a greater decrease in colony formation induced by K-Ras4a-G12V (75% decrease) than by K-Ras4a-G12V-3KR (45% decrease) (Figure 5).
evidence: Supported by soft agar colony formation assay data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Sirt2 KD more potently inhibited K-Ras4a-G12V-mediated colony formation than H-Ras4a-G12V-mediated colony formation.
source: Additionally, Sirt2 KD more potently inhibited K-Ras4a-G12V-mediated colony formation than H-Ras4a-G12V-mediated colony formation (Figure 5), consistent with the fact that SIRT2 regulates lysine fatty acylation of K-Ras4a but not H-Ras or K-Ras4a-3KR.
evidence: Supported by soft agar colony formation assay data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Lysine fatty acylation inhibits the ability of K-Ras4a-G12V to induce anchorage-independent growth of cells.
source: Thus, lysine fatty acylation inhibits the ability of K-Ras4a-G12V to induce anchorage-independent growth of cells and SIRT2 promotes it through defatty-acylation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the soft agar colony formation assay results shown in Figure 5.

claim: SIRT2 promotes the ability of K-Ras4a-G12V to induce anchorage-independent growth through defatty-acylation.
source: Thus, lysine fatty acylation inhibits the ability of K-Ras4a-G12V to induce anchorage-independent growth of cells and SIRT2 promotes it through defatty-acylation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the soft agar colony formation assay results shown in Figure 5.

claim: Neither the 3KR mutation nor SIRT2 KD affected EGF-stimulated GTP loading of K-Ras4a.
source: Neither the 3KR mutation nor SIRT2 KD affected EGF-stimulated GTP loading of K-Ras4a (Figure 6—figure supplement 1a and b) or the constitutively GTP-loaded state of K-Ras4a-G12V (Figure 6—figure supplement 1c and d).
evidence: Supported by RBD pull-down assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1a and b.

claim: Neither the 3KR mutation nor SIRT2 KD affected the constitutively GTP-loaded state of K-Ras4a-G12V.
source: Neither the 3KR mutation nor SIRT2 KD affected EGF-stimulated GTP loading of K-Ras4a (Figure 6—figure supplement 1a and b) or the constitutively GTP-loaded state of K-Ras4a-G12V (Figure 6—figure supplement 1c and d).
evidence: Supported by RBD pull-down assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1c and d.

claim: More colocalization of DsRed-RBD with K-Ras4a on intracellular puncta was observed in cells expressing the 3KR mutant than in cells expressing K-Ras4a-WT.
source: Notably, we observed more colocalization of DsRed-RBD with K-Ras4a on intracellular puncta in cells expressing the 3KR mutant (Figure 6—figure supplement 1e,f,g) than in cells expressing K-Ras4a-WT.
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1e, f, g.

claim: SIRT2 KD decreased the colocalization of DsRed-RBD with K-Ras4a-WT at intracellular puncta, but not with the 3KR mutant.
source: Furthermore, SIRT2 KD decreased the colocalization of DsRed-RBD with K-Ras4a-WT at intracellular puncta, but not with the 3KR mutant (Figure 6—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1e.

claim: SIRT2-dependent lysine defatty-acylation may promote the localization of activated (GTP-loaded) K-Ras4a at endomembranes.
source: The results above suggest that SIRT2-dependent lysine defatty-acylation may promote the localization of activated (GTP-loaded) K-Ras4a at endomembranes, which raises the possibility that lysine defatty-acylation may alter the signaling specificity of K-Ras4a by recruiting different effector proteins to endomembranes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the RBD colocalization results shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Neither the 3KR mutation nor Sirt2 KD altered the binding of K-Ras4a-G12V with Raf1, PI3K, or RalGDS.
source: Co-immunoprecipitation demonstrated that neither the 3KR mutation nor Sirt2 KD altered the binding of K-Ras4a-G12V with Raf1, PI3K, or RalGDS (Figure 6—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2a.

claim: SIRT2 catalyzed lysine defatty-acylation of K-Ras4a does not affect the activation of Raf1, PI3K or RalGDS by K-Ras4a.
source: These results suggest that SIRT2 catalyzed lysine defatty-acylation of K-Ras4a does not affect the activation of Raf1, PI3K or RalGDS by K-Ras4a.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the co-immunoprecipitation and signaling pathway activation data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: A greater interaction of A-Raf with K-Ras4a-G12V-3KR was observed than with K-Ras4a-G12V.
source: However, a greater interaction of A-Raf with K-Ras4a-G12V-3KR was observed than with K-Ras4a-G12V, and Sirt2 KD significantly decreased the interaction of A-Raf with K-Ras4a-G12V but not with K-Ras4a-G12V-3KR (Figure 6a and b).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6a and b.

claim: Sirt2 KD significantly decreased the interaction of A-Raf with K-Ras4a-G12V but not with K-Ras4a-G12V-3KR.
source: However, a greater interaction of A-Raf with K-Ras4a-G12V-3KR was observed than with K-Ras4a-G12V, and Sirt2 KD significantly decreased the interaction of A-Raf with K-Ras4a-G12V but not with K-Ras4a-G12V-3KR (Figure 6a and b).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6a and b.

claim: A-Raf is an effector protein of K-Ras4a that is regulated by lysine fatty acylation and SIRT2.
source: Thus, we concluded that A-Raf was an effector protein of K-Ras4a that was regulated by lysine fatty acylation and SIRT2.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6a and b.

claim: Sirt2 KD did not alter H-Ras-G12V-A-Raf interaction.
source: Unlike the effect of Sirt2 KD on K-Ras4a-G12V-A-Raf interaction, Sirt2 KD did not alter H-Ras-G12V-A-Raf interaction (Figure 6a and b).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6a and b.

claim: Neither 3KR mutation nor Sirt2 KD altered the binding of B-Raf to K-Ras4a-G12V.
source: We also assessed the interaction of K-Ras4a-G12V with another Raf family member, B-Raf. Co-IP indicated that neither 3KR mutation nor Sirt2 KD altered the binding of B-Raf to K-Ras4a-G12V (Figure 6—figure supplement 2c).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2c.

claim: Removal of lysine fatty acylation from K-Ras4a by SIRT2 results in its preferential association with A-Raf, but not B-Raf or C-Raf.
source: These results collectively demonstrate that removal of lysine fatty acylation from K-Ras4a by SIRT2 results in its preferential association with A-Raf, but not B-Raf or C-Raf.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6.

claim: K-Ras4a-G12V-3KR showed more colocalization with A-Raf on the endomembranes than K-Ras4a-G12V did.
source: Live cell imaging revealed that A-Raf colocalized with K-Ras4a-G12V at both the PM and endomembranes. K-Ras4a-G12V-3KR showed more colocalization with A-Raf on the endomembranes than K-Ras4a-G12V did.
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 6c and d.

claim: Sirt2 KD inhibited the endomembrane recruitment of A-Raf by K-Ras4a-G12V but not that by K-Ras4a-G12V-3KR.
source: Sirt2 KD inhibited the endomembrane recruitment of A-Raf by K-Ras4a-G12V but not that by K-Ras4a-G12V-3KR (Figure 6c and d).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 6c and d.

claim: Lysine defatty-acylation may facilitate the endomembrane recruitment of A-Raf by K-Ras4a.
source: It has been reported that the efficient activation of certain effector pathways by Ras is dependent on the entry of Ras to the endosomal compartment (Jura et al., 2006; Roy et al., 2002). Therefore, it is plausible that lysine defatty-acylation may facilitate the endomembrane recruitment of A-Raf by K-Ras4a, thereby increasing K-Ras4a transforming activity.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the colocalization results and previous literature.

claim: Inhibition of A-Raf expression with shRNA partially suppressed K-Ras4a-G12V-induced colony formation.
source: Inhibition of A-Raf expression with shRNA (Figure 6—figure supplement 4a) partially suppressed K-Ras4a-G12V-induced colony formation, indicating that A-Raf is important for K-Ras4a-G12V mediated transformation.
evidence: Supported by soft agar colony formation assay data shown in Figure 6e and Figure 6—figure supplement 4.

claim: A-Raf is important for K-Ras4a-G12V mediated transformation.
source: Inhibition of A-Raf expression with shRNA (Figure 6—figure supplement 4a) partially suppressed K-Ras4a-G12V-induced colony formation, indicating that A-Raf is important for K-Ras4a-G12V mediated transformation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the soft agar colony formation assay data shown in Figure 6e and Figure 6—figure supplement 4.

claim: A-Raf KD abrogated the 3KR mutation-mediated increase and Sirt2 KD-mediated decrease in the transformation activity of K-Ras4a-G12V.
source: Moreover, A-Raf KD abrogated the 3KR mutation-mediated increase and Sirt2 KD-mediated decrease in the transformation activity of K-Ras4a-G12V (Figure 6e and Figure 6—figure supplement 4b), suggesting that A-Raf is important for the regulation of K-Ras4a transforming activity by SIRT2-dependent lysine defatty-acylation.
evidence: Supported by soft agar colony formation assay data shown in Figure 6e and Figure 6—figure supplement 4b.

claim: A-Raf is important for the regulation of K-Ras4a transforming activity by SIRT2-dependent lysine defatty-acylation.
source: Moreover, A-Raf KD abrogated the 3KR mutation-mediated increase and Sirt2 KD-mediated decrease in the transformation activity of K-Ras4a-G12V (Figure 6e and Figure 6—figure supplement 4b), suggesting that A-Raf is important for the regulation of K-Ras4a transforming activity by SIRT2-dependent lysine defatty-acylation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the soft agar colony formation assay data shown in Figure 6e and Figure 6—figure supplement 4b.

claim: SIRT2-dependent lysine defatty-acylation enhances the recruitment of A-Raf to K-Ras4a at endomembranes, thereby promoting transforming activity of K-Ras4a.
source: These results further support the model that lysine defatty-acylation by SIRT2 enhances the recruitment of A-Raf to K-Ras4a at endomembranes, thereby promoting transforming activity of K-Ras4a.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the combined results from co-immunoprecipitation, colocalization, and soft agar colony formation assays shown in Figure 6.

claim: Mutations that activate Ras are found in about 30% of all human tumors screened.
source: Mutations that activate Ras are found in about 30% of all human tumors screened.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Ras mutations in cancer.

claim: KRAS mutations occur most frequently, accounting for 86% of RAS-driven cancers.
source: KRAS mutations, which affects both K-Ras4a and K-Ras4b, occur most frequently, accounting for 86% of RAS-driven cancers (Cox et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: K-Ras4a is widely expressed in human cancers.
source: Recent studies showed that K-Ras4a is widely expressed in human cancers, suggesting that K-Ras4a plays a significant role in KRAS-driven tumors (Tsai et al., 2015; Zhao et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: K-Ras4a plays a significant role in KRAS-driven tumors.
source: Recent studies showed that K-Ras4a is widely expressed in human cancers, suggesting that K-Ras4a plays a significant role in KRAS-driven tumors (Tsai et al., 2015; Zhao et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an inference based on the expression data cited.

claim: Depletion of SIRT2 increased lysine fatty acylation and diminished transforming activity of K-Ras4a.
source: Our findings reveal that K-Ras4a is regulated by SIRT2-dependent lysine defatty-acylation. Depletion of SIRT2 increased lysine fatty acylation and diminished transforming activity of K-Ras4a, suggesting that interference with K-Ras4a lysine fatty acylation could be an approach to anti-K-Ras therapy.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from the study.

claim: Interference with K-Ras4a lysine fatty acylation could be an approach to anti-K-Ras therapy.
source: Our findings reveal that K-Ras4a is regulated by SIRT2-dependent lysine defatty-acylation. Depletion of SIRT2 increased lysine fatty acylation and diminished transforming activity of K-Ras4a, suggesting that interference with K-Ras4a lysine fatty acylation could be an approach to anti-K-Ras therapy.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the findings of the study.

claim: The known biological functions of sirtuins have been mainly attributed to their deacetylase activities.
source: So far, the known biological functions of sirtuins have been mainly attributed to their deacetylase activities.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The biological significance of sirtuins as lysine deacylases remains largely unknown.
source: Although sirtuins are increasingly recognized as lysine deacylases in addition to deacetylases, the biological significance of sirtuins as lysine deacylases remains largely unknown (Bheda et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: This work identifies the first physiological defatty-acylation substrate for SIRT2.
source: Our work here identifies the first physiological defatty-acylation substrate for SIRT2.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings.

claim: SIRT2 may provide a link between K-Ras4a signaling and cellular metabolism.
source: Since protein acyl lysine modifications likely use acyl-CoA molecules as the acyl donors, the cellular metabolic state can affect acyl lysine PTMs by altering the concentration of acyl-CoA molecules. Sirtuins requires NAD as a co-substrate and the NAD level is regulated by cellular metabolism. Thus SIRT2 may provide an additional link between K-Ras4a signaling and cellular metabolism.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the known biochemistry of acylation and sirtuin reactions.

claim: SIRT2, as a Ras regulator, may be an important therapeutic target for cancer.
source: Given that Ras proteins play critical roles in many human cancers, SIRT2, as a Ras regulator, may be an important therapeutic target for cancer, which is consistent with several recent reports (Jing et al., 2016; Moniot et al., 2017; Shah et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2014; Wilking-Busch et al., 2017; Xu et al., 2016; Zhao et al., 2013, 2016).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citations to recent literature.
